title: Product of Array Except Self
description: Brute force to optimized: recomputing the product per position versus prefix and suffix arrays versus reusing the output array.

blocks.text: Given an array nums, return an array answer where answer[i] equals the product of every element in nums except nums[i]. This must be solved without using the division operator, and ideally in O(n) time.

blocks.title: Analogy: Everyone's Contribution Except Their Own
blocks.text: Imagine splitting a group photo credit where each person's number represents how much they contributed, and each person wants to know the combined contribution of everyone else in the room, excluding themselves.

blocks.caption: Each output position needs the product of every other value, without dividing

blocks.text: With just two elements, each output position is simply the other single value, giving [2, 1].
The instruction "without division" is not an arbitrary restriction, it is a strong hint about which technique the problem wants.

blocks.title: How Should We Think?
blocks.text:
Observation 1: The obvious shortcut, total product divided by nums[i], is explicitly banned, and would also break the moment any value is 0, since division by zero is undefined.

Observation 2: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock already showed the power of a single running value swept across the array (a running minimum), rather than rescanning from scratch for every position.

Observation 3: Here, that idea splits into two separate running products, everything strictly to the left of a position, and everything strictly to the right of it. Precomputing both in one pass each, then multiplying them together, replaces the O(n squared) rescanning entirely.

Observation 4: Since the problem already requires an output array of size n, that same array can be reused as the prefix products storage, and the suffix side can shrink down to a single running variable swept from right to left, exactly the same "one running value, one pass" instinct as the stock problem, just applied twice.
Treating "no division allowed" as a signal to precompute left and right products, rather than as a mere inconvenience, is what leads directly to the prefix and suffix product pattern.
For every position, multiply together every other value by scanning the rest of the array.

items: For every index i, start a running product at 1.
Multiply in every value at index j not equal to i.
Store that running product as answer[i].

codes.python:
def product_except_self(nums):
    n = len(nums)
    answer = [1] * n
    for i in range(n):                                      # for every output position
        product = 1
        for j in range(n):                                    # multiply in every other value
            if j != i:
                product *= nums[j]
        answer[i] = product
    return answer


if __name__ == "__main__":
    nums = [1, 2, 3, 4]
    print(product_except_self(nums))

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Every output position rescans the entire array, deliberately skipping only its own index, so no product is ever reused between positions.
A long running product is used in the Java and C++ versions to avoid overflow while accumulating, only narrowed to a 32 bit int at the very end.
The result is correct and never touches division, but recomputes overlapping work at every single position.

blocks.text: Every position correctly multiplies together every value except its own, so the result is correct and never uses division.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared), an inner scan of the whole array for every output position.
Space: O(1) extra, not counting the output array.

Limitation: the product to the left of a position and the product to the right of it are each recomputed from scratch for every single output position, when they could instead be built up once and reused.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why the brute force works but is wasteful: the product to the left of a position and the product to the right of it are each rebuilt from nothing at every position, even though most of that work is shared between neighboring positions.

What a prefix and suffix pass fixes directly: build a prefix products array where prefix[i] holds the product of everything before i, and a suffix products array where suffix[i] holds the product of everything after i, each in a single left to right or right to left pass.

Can the suffix array itself be avoided: yes, once the output array already holds the prefix products, the suffix side only ever needs a single running value swept backward, not a whole second array.

The core idea: answer[i] is exactly prefix[i] times suffix[i], so precomputing each side once, in one pass apiece, replaces the O(n squared) rescanning with two O(n) passes.

The product except self at position i is exactly the product of everything to its left multiplied by the product of everything to its right. Both of those can be precomputed in a single pass each: a prefix products array where prefix[i] holds the product of everything before i, and a suffix products array where suffix[i] holds the product of everything after i. Multiplying the two together at each position gives the answer directly.
Build a prefix product array and a suffix product array, then multiply them position by position.

blocks.caption: Optimized: multiply a prefix products array with a suffix products array

blocks.text: This works because every value in nums lies either strictly to the left or strictly to the right of any given position, never both, so multiplying the complete left side product by the complete right side product accounts for every other value exactly once, with no overlap and no omission.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), one pass to build each array plus one pass to combine them.
Space: O(n), for the prefix and suffix arrays, on top of the O(n) output array.
10. Further Optimization: Reusing the Output Array

The suffix array does not need to exist as its own separate array. The output array can first be filled with prefix products directly, and then a second pass from the right, keeping just a single running suffix product variable instead of a whole array, can multiply that running value into each position as it goes. This drops the extra space down to a single variable, beyond the output array the problem already requires.

blocks.caption: Further optimization: fill prefix products in place, then sweep a single running suffix variable

items: The first left to right pass fills the output array with prefix products directly, exactly as the standalone prefix array did before.
The second right to left pass multiplies each position by a single running suffix product, then updates that running value with the current element, never needing a whole second array.
By the end, every position holds prefix[i] times suffix[i], identical to the two array version, but using only one extra variable beyond the required output array.

Time: O(n), the same two passes.
Space: O(1) extra, beyond the output array the problem already requires.

blocks.text: This problem is the classic introduction to the prefix and suffix product pattern, and its further round shows how the output array itself can double as scratch space, a trick worth watching for whenever a problem already requires an output array of the same size as the input.

items: Reaching for division, total product divided by nums[i], which the problem explicitly forbids, and which also breaks whenever any element is zero.
Forgetting to handle zeros carefully, though the prefix and suffix approach naturally produces the correct 0 results without any special casing.

blocks.text: Mention the division based approach first to show awareness of it, then explain clearly why it is disallowed (division by zero, and the constraint itself forbids it) before moving to the prefix and suffix product approach.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text:
If the interviewer says "can you do this without any extra array", think: fill the output array with prefix products, then sweep a single running suffix variable from the right.
If the interviewer says "what if the array contains a zero", think: the prefix and suffix approach already handles it correctly, with no special casing needed.
If the interviewer says "why can't you just divide", think: division is explicitly forbidden and breaks entirely whenever any value is 0.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: Brute force: O(n squared) time, O(1) extra space. Optimized: O(n) time, O(n) extra space. Further optimized: O(n) time, O(1) extra space beyond the output array.

items: Pattern: prefix and suffix products, later folded into the output array itself as scratch space.

Core Idea: answer[i] is exactly the product of everything strictly before i multiplied by everything strictly after i, so precomputing both sides once replaces rescanning the array for every position.
Time: O(n squared) for the brute force, O(n) for both optimized versions.
Space: O(1) extra for the brute force, O(n) extra for the separate prefix and suffix arrays, O(1) extra once the output array is reused.
Most Important Observation: the "no division" constraint is a direct signal to precompute left and right products, and an already-required output array can double as scratch space.
Interview Difficulty: the prefix and suffix idea is easy to state; folding the suffix pass into the output array in place is what shows a deeper grasp of space optimization.
One line memory trick: answer equals prefix times suffix, and the output array can hold the prefix products itself.
